## Why This Is Asked
This question tests practical gate design for data contracts, schema evolution, and data quality in a real-world Delta Lake context.

## Key Concepts
- Data contracts and schema evolution
- Delta Lake baseline/versioning
- Great Expectations data quality

```yaml
# GitHub Actions sample (high level)
name: Delta Gate
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  gate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Schema diff
        run: bash scripts/compare_schemas.sh

        run: make ge
      - name: Apply policy
        run: kubectl apply -f policy.yaml
```

- How would you handle concurrent PRs affecting the same schema?
- How to measure impact of schema changes on downstream pipelines?

## Why This Is Asked

- cosign signing and repo public keys
- SBOMs (CycloneDX)
- central provenance store and attestations

## Code Example
```yaml
name: Sign-and-attest
on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]
jobs:
  build-and-sign:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Build image
        run: docker build -t my-registry/svc:$GITHUB_SHA .
      - name: cosign sign
        run: cosign sign --key cosign.pub my-registry/svc:$GITHUB_SHA
      - name: generate SBOM
        run: cyclonedx-bom -o bom.xml my-registry/svc:$GITHUB_SHA
      - name: upload SBOM
        run: curl -X POST -F file=@bom.xml https://provenance-store.local/upload
```

questions.explanation:
Why This Is Asked
- Tests policy-as-code skills for multi-tenant Kubernetes environments
- Evaluates ability to translate security requirements into enforceable runtime and CI gates

Key Concepts
- Kyverno, Pod Security Standards, Resource limits, CI gates, Drift detection

Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-secure-deployments
spec:
  validationFailureAction: enforce
  background: true
  rules:
  - name: security-context
    match:
      resources:
        kinds: ["Deployment"]
    validate:
      message: "Each container must define a secure securityContext with runAsNonRoot: true, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, and drop all capabilities"
      pattern:
        spec:
          template:
            spec:
              containers:
              - securityContext:
                  runAsNonRoot: "true"
                  readOnlyRootFilesystem: "true"
                  capabilities:
                    drop: ["ALL"]
  - name: require-resources
    match:
      resources:
        kinds: ["Deployment"]
    validate:
      message: "Each container must specify resource limits and requests"
      pattern:
        spec:
          template:
            spec:
              containers:
              - resources:
                  limits:
                    memory: "?*"
                    cpu: "?*"
                  requests:
                    memory: "?*"
                    cpu: "?*"
```

Failing Test Manifest
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: insecure-app
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: insecure
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: nginx:latest
```

Passing Test Manifest
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: secure-app
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: secure
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: nginx:latest
        securityContext:
          runAsNonRoot: true
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
          capabilities:
            drop: ["ALL"]
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "64Mi"
            cpu: "250m"
          limits:
            memory: "128Mi"
            cpu: "500m"
```

CI Validation Steps
```bash
# Install Kyverno CLI
brew install kyverno

# Validate policies against manifests
kyverno apply policy.yaml --manifest deployment.yaml

# CI/CD integration example (GitHub Actions)
- name: Validate Kubernetes manifests
  run: |
    kyverno apply policy.yaml -f deploy/
```

Runtime Gate Demonstration
```bash
# Apply the policy cluster-wide
kubectl apply -f policy.yaml

# Verify policy is active
kubectl get clusterpolicy require-secure-deployments

# Attempt to deploy non-compliant manifest (will fail)
kubectl apply -f insecure-deployment.yaml
# Error: Validation failed: Each container must define a secure securityContext...

# Deploy compliant manifest (will succeed)
kubectl apply -f secure-deployment.yaml
# deployment.apps/secure-app created
```

questions.explanation:
Why This Is Asked
- Tests ability to translate governance requirements into concrete, enforceable policies and CI steps. 
- Combines data catalog metadata with image provenance and basic security gates in a beginner-friendly way.

Key Concepts
- Policy as code (Kyverno/OPA Gatekeeper)
- Annotations for data governance (data-catalog.uri)
- Image provenance (digest pinning, registry allowlist)
- Basic hardening (forbidden hostNetwork/hostPath, non-privileged)
- Namespace quotas and network policies

Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: Policy
metadata:
  name: governance-baseline
spec:
  rules:
  - name: require-data-catalog
    match:
      resources:
        kinds: ["Deployment", "StatefulSet"]
    validate:
      message: "data.catalog.uri annotation required"
      pattern:
        metadata:
          annotations:
            data.catalog.uri: "?*"
  - name: require-image-digest
    match:
      resources:
        kinds: ["Deployment", "StatefulSet"]
    validate:
      message: "image must be pinned with digest"
      pattern:
        spec:
          template:
            spec:
              containers:
              - image: "*@sha256:*"
  - name: disallow-risky-fields
    match:
      resources:
        kinds: ["Pod", "Deployment", "StatefulSet"]
    prune: false
    validate:
      message: "hostNetwork/hostPath/privileged not allowed"
      pattern:
        spec:
          hostNetwork: False
        volumes: []
```

Failing Manifest (example)
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: data-processor
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    spec:
      hostNetwork: true
      volumes:
        - name: data
          hostPath:
            path: /data
      containers:
        - name: processor
          image: registry.internal/data-processor:latest
```

Passing Manifest (example)
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: data-processor
  namespace: team-a
  annotations:
    data.catalog.uri: "https://catalog.example.org/datasets/123"
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: processor
          image: registry.internal/data-processor@sha256:abcdef123456...
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "100m"
              memory: "128Mi"
              limits:
              cpu: "200m"
              memory: "256Mi"
```

Follow-up notes
- How would you test the policy in CI (e.g., kyverno test, simulate PRs)?
- How to handle exceptions per-namespace while preserving governance?

## Why This Is Asked
This question rigorously tests practical CI security knowledge for multi-tenant infrastructure, covering both container images and WASM modules deployed across edge and cloud environments. It evaluates understanding of supply chain security, provenance verification, and admission control policies.

- Security: Istio mTLS (PeerAuthentication), NetworkPolicy for egress control
- CI verification: conftest for policy testing, kubeval for manifest validation, dry-run kubectl apply

## CI Verification Steps
1. **Policy Validation**: Use `conftest test k8s-manifests/ -p policy.rego` to verify compliance
2. **Manifest Validation**: Run `kubeval manifests/*.yaml` against Kubernetes schemas
3. **Dry Run**: Execute `kubectl apply --dry-run=client -f manifests/` to test admission
4. **Network Policy Test**: Use `kubectl get networkpolicy -n <tenant-ns>` to verify egress restrictions
5. **ServiceAccount Audit**: Check `kubectl auth can-i --as=<serviceaccount> <verb> <resource>` for least privilege

This comprehensive approach ensures every namespace meets security requirements before deployment, with automated CI gates preventing policy violations.

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

This question evaluates practical understanding of Kubernetes security primitives including RBAC, ServiceAccount isolation, PodSecurityContext, and admission controls—essential skills for securing containerized workloads.

## Key Concepts

- **Namespace-scoped RBAC**: Role and RoleBinding for resource access control within specific namespaces
- **ServiceAccount isolation**: Dedicated service accounts to separate pod identities and permissions
- **PodSecurityContext**: Security constraints including runAsNonRoot, runAsUser, readOnlyRootFilesystem, and capability dropping
- **Admission controls**: PodSecurity standards and OPA Gatekeeper for policy enforcement at admission time

## Code Example

```yaml
# ServiceAccount (dev)
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: data-processor-sa
  namespace: dev
---
# Role for read-only access to ConfigMaps and Secrets
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: data-processor-role
  namespace: dev
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["configmaps", "secrets"]
  verbs: ["get", "list"]
---
# RoleBinding
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: data-processor-binding
  namespace: dev
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: data-processor-sa
  namespace: dev
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: data-processor-role
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
```
